catalog_quote: The lexical tones in Table 10 indicate that Tegem is a tone language, i.e., tones are used to create lexical distinctions while affixation is used for grammatical distinction. The language most frequently uses the two level tones (H/L) and then the two contour tones (F/R). The other two contour tones (FR/RF) are used occasionally and they contrast with the other two contour tones, e.g., FR in ʈîí ‘pile of soil’ and F in ʈíì ‘kind of grass’; RF in ʈǐìl ‘cowbird’ and R in ʈìíl ‘acacia wood’. The tone domain (TBU: tone-bearing unit) in Tegem is the syllable as change of one syllable tone changes the word meaning, i.e., ‘in a tone language each syllable of a word will have its own tone.’ (Dixon 2009:279). ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Tegem (Lafofa) is described as a lexical tone language (H, L, falling, rising; FR/RF on long/extra-long vowels; syllable = TBU). The thesis, the only modern phonological description, says nothing at all about word stress or accent. The only stress remark in the literature reachable here is Stevenson's group-level observation (via Tucker & Bryan 1966, ch. 18a sec. 2b, covering Koalib-Moro, Talodi-Masakin and Lafofa together) that 'dynamic stress, accompanied by High or Low tone, plays a greater role than syllabic pitch as such, but is not equally prominent in all languages' -- with no stress position given and nothing specific to Lafofa.
new_statements.exceptions: None; tone/length alternations under suffixation of -go / -i ('this') noted (p. 60); disyllabic noun roots disallow two contour tones or two different level tones (Table 11).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (elicited citation forms of lexical items from two main consultants, one from Tekeim village, one from the Eliri plain villages near Lafofa; recorded in Khartoum). Author explicitly defers post-lexical/phrasal tonology.
new_statements.identity_note: Sosal 2018 describes Tegem (endonym; = Lafofa of Stevenson/Ethnologue, ISO laf, Glottolog lafo1243; Glottolog 5.x places it under a 'Tegem' node tege1244). Data from two main consultants, one from Jebel Tekeim (the 'Jebel Tekeim' dialect of older sources) and one from the Eliri plain villages near Lafofa village, recorded in Khartoum; author treats Tekeim/Lafofa differences as sub-phonemic. El Amira (amir1234-type variety, 'Amira') is explicitly excluded as a separate language. The Tucker & Bryan / Stevenson stress remark is group-level (Koalib-Moro + Talodi-Masakin + Lafofa), not Lafofa-specific.

sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 4.4 'Tone' (pp. 59-60) and 5.5 (p. 77) establish lexical tone (H, L, F, R, plus FR/RF; TBU = syllable; 'Tegem is a tone language'); the words stress/accent/prominence do not occur outside the bibliography. Suprasegmental chapter covers syllable types, vowel harmony and tone only.
